mcqs.question: Why does querying a regular (non-materialized) view give you data that's always up to date?
options: The view stores no data of its own — it re-runs its underlying query against the live base tables on every access
The database automatically refreshes the view's stored data every few seconds
Regular views are only allowed on tables that never change
The view keeps a change log that it replays before returning results
mcqs.explanation: A regular view is just a saved query definition; every access substitutes it into the live query against base tables, so there's no staleness possible. There's no automatic timed refresh, no restriction to unchanging tables, and no change log involved.

mcqs.question: Why can't you typically INSERT through a view that joins two tables together?
options: INSERT is disabled on all views regardless of their definition
Joined views require a special license in most database engines
The engine cannot unambiguously determine which base table's row the new data belongs to
Views can only be created from tables, never from joins, so this view would fail to even be created
mcqs.explanation: Updatability requires the view to map cleanly back to one base table's rows; a join makes that mapping ambiguous, so most engines reject or restrict writes through it. Simple single-table views do support INSERT; joined views are perfectly valid to create, just not always writable.

mcqs.question: A dashboard runs an expensive five-table aggregation query thousands of times a day, and slightly stale data (a few minutes old) is acceptable. What's the better fit?
options: A regular view, since it always returns fresh data
Neither — views should never be used for aggregations
A regular view with an added ORDER BY to speed it up
A materialized view, refreshed on a schedule, since it trades slight staleness for fast reads
mcqs.explanation: A materialized view is exactly the tool for an expensive, frequently-read query where some staleness is tolerable — it caches the result instead of recomputing it each time. A regular view would re-run the full expensive aggregation on every read; ORDER BY doesn't address the underlying cost.

mcqs.question: Why can stacking view C on view B on view A produce a query plan that's much harder to optimize than expected?
options: Each view in the stack is executed as a fully separate transaction
Views can only be nested up to two levels before the database rejects the query
Because views are inlined at query time, the final executed query is the full merged expansion of all three definitions, which can confuse the optimizer
Nested views always force a full table scan on every underlying table
mcqs.explanation: Regular views get inlined into the outer query, so nesting several compounds into one large expanded query that can be genuinely hard for the optimizer to simplify well. There's no hard nesting limit, no forced full scans, and no separate transaction per view layer.

mcqs.question: A team wants analysts to query customer data without ever seeing the salary column or rows outside their assigned region. What's a common way to enforce this at the database layer?
options: Ask analysts to manually add a WHERE clause and avoid selecting the salary column in every query
Encrypt the entire customers table and give analysts the decryption key
Grant analysts SELECT on a view that excludes the salary column and filters rows by region, and revoke their direct table access
Create a separate physical copy of the table for each analyst
mcqs.explanation: A restricted view combined with revoking direct table access enforces the policy at the database layer, independent of what any individual query does. Relying on analysts to self-restrict is fragile; encrypting the whole table doesn't achieve column/row-level restriction; per-analyst physical copies don't scale and go stale.

mcqs.question: A materialized view was created six months ago with no refresh job ever configured. What has likely happened to its data?
options: It has automatically stayed in sync with the base tables the whole time
It is frozen at whatever the base tables looked like at creation time, and has silently drifted from reality since
The database would have refused to create it without a refresh schedule
It refreshes itself once a day by default on every major engine
mcqs.explanation: Materialized views never refresh automatically — without an explicit REFRESH call, the data is frozen at its last refresh (here, creation time) and silently goes stale with no error. Most engines happily create one with no schedule attached, and there's no universal daily-default behavior.
